claims.claim: In API-key mode the proxy reads the key from stdin, formats it as `Bearer <key>` and attempts to mlock(2) the memory holding that header.
claims.explanation: The key is read with read(2) into a stack buffer prefixed with "Bearer ", copied into a leaked String and mlocked. mlock failure is ignored, which matches the README's word 'attempts'.
claims.note: On Windows mlock_str is a no-op; the README only says 'attempts'.

source.quote: By default reads the API key from `stdin`.

claims.claim: Dump files redact `Authorization` and any header whose name includes `cookie`; other header values are dumped in full.
claims.explanation: Both request and response header conversions call should_redact_header, which redacts Authorization and any header containing 'cookie'.

source.quote: Header values are dumped in full except `Authorization` and any header whose name includes `cookie`, which are redacted.

claims.claim: The proxy accepts exactly POST /v1/responses (no query string) and answers everything else with 403, apart from the optional GET /shutdown.
claims.explanation: The path comparison is exact (so a query string fails it), and /shutdown is only handled when --http-shutdown is set.

source.quote:

requests are rejected with `403 Forbidden`, except for the optional shutdown
endpoint described below.

claims.explanation: Validation, the String copy and the zeroize of the stack buffer all happen as described.

claims.claim: Rollout tracing is not telemetry: nothing is uploaded, and local bundles are written only when CODEX_ROLLOUT_TRACE_ROOT is set.
claims.explanation: Tracing starts only when the env var is set, otherwise a disabled context is used. The crate depends only on the `http` types crate and no HTTP client, and its only entry point writes to the local root directory.

source.quote:
> **Privacy:** Rollout tracing is not telemetry. Codex does **not** upload or
> report these traces; it writes local bundles only when
> `CODEX_ROLLOUT_TRACE_ROOT` is set.

claims.claim: The TUI writes a plaintext log only when `log_dir` is set explicitly; otherwise it keeps diagnostics in bounded local stores.
claims.explanation: The file layer is created only if log_dir is present in the effective config or requirements; the file is opened with mode 0600 on Unix and named codex-tui.log.
claims.note: I did not audit the 'bounded local stores' (state DB / feedback ring buffer) beyond seeing they exist.

source.quote: The TUI records diagnostics in bounded local stores by default. Set `log_dir` explicitly to enable a plaintext TUI log for a run:

claims.claim: Under bubblewrap the helper isolates the user namespace and (by default) the PID namespace, mounts the filesystem read-only via `--ro-bind / /`, and blocks io_uring in all seccomp filter modes.
claims.explanation: The io_uring denials are unconditional; user and PID namespaces are unshared as described.
claims.note: `--ro-bind / /` is used when the policy has full-disk read access; for restricted-read policies it starts from an empty filesystem with scoped read-only mounts (bwrap.rs:516-517). Both are read-only by default.

source.quote:
All filter
  modes block `io_uring` to prevent bypassing socket-family restrictions.
- When bubblewrap is active, the filesystem is read-only by default via `--ro-bind / /`.

claims.claim: Setting CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM to false (0 and no also accepted) forces GitHub Releases; the installers default to releases.openai.com and fall back to GitHub.
claims.explanation: Both scripts read the variable and fall back to GitHub when releases.openai.com is unavailable. In install.ps1 only 1/true/yes enable the preference, so false, 0 and no disable it.
claims.note: Did not independently inspect install.sh's value parsing at line 9 beyond the variable being read.

source.quote: The standalone installers download from `https://releases.openai.com/codex` by default and fall back to GitHub Releases if a metadata or asset download is unavailable.

evidence.quote: warn "releases.openai.com is unavailable; falling back to GitHub Releases."

claims.claim: The standalone installers (macOS/Linux and Windows) download from releases.openai.com by default.
claims.explanation: In the repo, install.sh defaults the preference to false and uses GitHub Releases unless the variable is 1/true/yes; install.ps1 defaults to true. The hosted chatgpt.com script may differ from this copy.
claims.user_impact: A Mac/Linux user running the repository's install.sh who expects downloads from releases.openai.com gets GitHub Releases unless they set CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM=true. Only the Windows script defaults to releases.openai.com. This corrects my earlier claim #8, which wrongly treated the default as releases.openai.com.

source.quote: The standalone installers download from `https://releases.openai.com/codex` by default and fall back to GitHub Releases if a metadata or asset download is unavailable.

review.reason: README says installers default to releases.openai.com, but install.sh defaults the preference to false (GitHub Releases) while only install.ps1 defaults to true. Real mismatch for Mac/Linux; low severity is appropriate.

claims.claim: By default the TypeScript SDK's Codex CLI inherits the Node.js process environment; passing `env` fully replaces it, and the SDK still injects required variables such as CODEX_API_KEY.
claims.explanation: With env given, only it is used; otherwise process.env is copied. The SDK adds the originator variable, CODEX_API_KEY when an apiKey is set, and PATH directories for the bundled binary.
claims.note: The SDK also always sets an internal originator variable and may prepend PATH entries, beyond just CODEX_API_KEY.

source.quote:
By default, the Codex CLI inherits the Node.js process environment. Provide the optional `env` parameter when instantiating the
`Codex` client to fully control which variables the CLI receives

claims.claim: Raw `configOverrides` are applied after structured `config` overrides, and SDK-managed settings like `baseUrl` and thread options are applied after both.
claims.explanation: The argument order is structured config, then raw overrides, then baseUrl and thread options such as web_search and approval_policy, so later --config flags win on duplicates.
claims.note: Precedence among repeated --config flags is determined by the CLI, which I did not trace; the SDK's emission order matches the README.

source.quote:
Raw overrides are applied after structured `config` overrides and take precedence over them. SDK-managed settings, such as
`baseUrl`, and thread-specific options are applied afterward and take precedence.

claims.explanation: package.json engines declares node >=18, matching the README.

source.quote: Requires Node.js 18+.

claims.explanation: Non-HTTPS endpoints are rejected unless they are http on loopback, and then only for an unmanaged, unrestricted network policy; that path builds a direct client with no proxy. Redirects are disabled and the 150s and 64 MiB limits match.

source.quote:
HTTPS is required except for direct loopback HTTP with an unrestricted, unmanaged
factory. This exception bypasses proxies to keep plaintext credentials local.

claims.explanation: The URL scheme must be https, the federated client uses no-redirect policy, and the credential buffers use Zeroizing plus sensitive headers, as documented. The README is honest that the destination host is not verified.

source.quote:
URL. It requires HTTPS and refuses redirects, but it does not verify that GitHub
owns the destination.

claims.explanation: On WSL1 the sandbox transform returns an error when the policy needs bubblewrap, before any bwrap invocation.

source.quote:
- WSL1 is not supported for bubblewrap sandboxing; Codex rejects sandboxed
  shell commands that would require the bubblewrap path before invoking `bwrap`.

claims.explanation: The WebSocket upgrade handler authorizes each connection against the policy built from the shared websocket-auth settings; without flags the default settings apply no authentication, which the README calls opt-in.

source.quote: Direct WebSocket listeners support app-server's opt-in auth flags, including `--ws-auth capability-token --ws-token-sha256 HEX`, token files, and signed bearer tokens

claims.claim: The proxy can authenticate with short-lived OpenAI credentials obtained by exchanging a GitHub Actions OIDC identity token.
claims.explanation: The federated path performs an RFC 8693 token exchange of the GitHub-minted JWT at auth.openai.com and uses the returned access token as the bearer credential.
claims.note: Whether the exchange succeeds depends on an OpenAI-side workload identity configuration outside the repo.

source.quote: short-lived OpenAI credentials obtained through GitHub Actions OIDC.

claims.claim: With --http-shutdown, an unprivileged user can make a GET to /shutdown to stop the proxy, as designed.
claims.explanation: The shutdown endpoint has no authentication and any local process that can reach 127.0.0.1 can stop the proxy; the README states this openly. The same holds for using the proxy: any local user can send Responses requests that are authenticated with the privileged user's key.

source.quote: Though if `--http-shutdown` is specified, an unprivileged user _can_ make a `GET` request to `/shutdown` to shutdown the server

claims.claim: In OIDC mode the proxy uses sensitive HTTP headers and zeroizes temporary credential buffers.
claims.explanation: The temporary Bearer buffer is Zeroizing and the header is marked sensitive, as stated.

source.quote: OIDC mode uses sensitive HTTP headers and zeroizes temporary credential

claims.claim: Authentication is `Authorization: Bearer <key>` in API-key mode and `Authorization: Bearer <OpenAI access token>` in OIDC mode; the incoming Authorization header is never forwarded.
claims.explanation: Client-supplied Authorization and Host headers are dropped and replaced by the proxy's Bearer header in both modes.

source.quote: - Authentication is `Authorization: Bearer <key>` in API-key mode and `Authorization: Bearer <OpenAI access token>` in OIDC mode.

claims.claim: The standalone network proxy enables HTTPS MITM automatically for limited mode or when MITM hooks are configured, and `mitm` otherwise defaults to false.
claims.explanation: The standalone loader ORs mitm with limited mode or non-empty hooks; the Codex permissions path does the same in permissions_toml.rs. Lower-level validation requires mitm=true whenever hooks exist, which this auto-enable satisfies.

source.quote:
`mitm` defaults to `false`. `mitm_ca` defaults to `None` and is omitted from serialized JSON when
unset. HTTPS MITM is enabled automatically for limited mode or configured `mitm_hooks`. Set `mitm` to
`true` to enable it explicitly.

claims.claim: In OIDC mode, stdin supplies GitHub's ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, not the minted JWT or an OpenAI API key.
claims.explanation: The OIDC source reads the request credential from stdin and sends it as the Authorization header of the GitHub request-URL call to mint subject tokens; the OpenAI access token comes from the exchange.

source.quote:
In this mode, stdin supplies GitHub's `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN`, **not**
the minted GitHub OIDC JWT or an OpenAI API key.

behaviors.behavior: Codex sends product analytics events to the ChatGPT backend (<chatgpt_base_url>/codex/analytics-events/events) whenever the user is signed in with ChatGPT/Codex-backend auth (and a reduced set of event types with API-key auth). The analytics queue is created unless analytics.enabled is explicitly false, so it is on by default.
behaviors.user_impact: Users who read the README, install guide or SECURITY.md are never told that usage analytics are collected by default or that analytics.enabled = false in config.toml opts out. The opt-out is only visible in a code comment on the config struct.
behaviors.docs_searched: README.md, docs/install.md, docs/config.md, docs/authentication.md, docs/sandbox.md, SECURITY.md and a repo-wide case-insensitive search of every *.md for 'analytics': only codex-rs/app-server-test-client/README.md (a test tool) mentions it; none of the user-facing docs describe default analytics or the opt-out.

evidence.quote: /// When `false`, disables OpenAI analytics across Codex product surfaces in this profile.

review.reason: Analytics queue is created unless analytics.enabled is explicitly false, so it is on by default and posts to the ChatGPT backend. User-facing docs searched do not disclose it or the opt-out. Medium severity is reasonable, though possibly slightly high since it is tied to signed-in use.

behaviors.behavior: In release builds, OTel metrics are exported by default to OpenAI's Statsig endpoint (https://ab.chatgpt.com/otlp/v1/metrics) with an embedded client API key. The default metrics_exporter is Statsig and it follows analytics.enabled; debug builds turn it off. This also means the otel README claim I recorded as #12 ('no otel exporter is configured by default') is true only for the log and trace exporters, not for metrics.
behaviors.user_impact: Users are not told that release builds send metrics to a Statsig-backed endpoint by default, or that analytics.enabled = false or otel.metrics_exporter = "none" stops it. The otel README only describes Statsig as a 'shorthand', not as the default.
behaviors.docs_searched: README.md, docs/install.md, docs/config.md, SECURITY.md, codex-rs/otel/README.md (mentions Statsig only as an available exporter shorthand at lines 187-190, not as the default) and a repo-wide search of *.md for statsig/analytics.

evidence.quote:
/// Metrics exporter. Defaults to `statsig`, which follows `analytics.enabled`.
    /// Custom OTLP exporters are independent of `analytics.enabled`; `none` disables metrics export.

review.reason: Metrics exporter defaults to Statsig (an OpenAI endpoint) when unset, and docs only mention Statsig as an available shorthand. Undisclosed default telemetry. Overlaps with b1; severity medium is acceptable but could be low.

raw_claims.claim: With --http-shutdown, an unprivileged user can make a GET to /shutdown to stop the proxy, as designed.
raw_claims.explanation: The shutdown endpoint has no authentication and any local process that can reach 127.0.0.1 can stop the proxy; the README states this openly. raw_claims.claim: Authentication is `Authorization: Bearer <key>` in API-key mode and `Authorization: Bearer <OpenAI access token>` in OIDC mode; the incoming Authorization header is never forwarded.
raw_claims.explanation: Client-supplied Authorization and Host headers are dropped and replaced by the proxy's Bearer header in both modes.

raw_claims.claim: The standalone network proxy enables HTTPS MITM automatically for limited mode or when MITM hooks are configured, and `mitm` otherwise defaults to false.
raw_claims.explanation: The standalone loader ORs mitm with limited mode or non-empty hooks; the Codex permissions path does the same in permissions_toml.rs. Lower-level validation requires mitm=true whenever hooks exist, which this auto-enable satisfies.

source.quote:
`mitm` defaults to `false`. `mitm_ca` defaults to `None` and is omitted from serialized JSON when
unset. HTTPS MITM is enabled automatically for limited mode or configured `mitm_hooks`. Set `mitm` to
`true` to enable it explicitly.
